title: A difficulty: free first act, yet merely passive
source_text: LXIII. Porro quod fatentur Scholae Reformatae Doctores, hominem qui per Dei gratiam convertitur, libere ipsum primum conversionis actum elicere, prima specie satis concordare non videtur, cum eo quod communiter docent, idque cum Theologis confessionis Augustanae, videlicet, hominem ad opus regenerationis & conversionis suae mere passive se habere. Quomodo enim voluntas humana potest conversionis actum libere elicere, & simul tamen ad sui conversionem mere passive se habere? an mere passive se habet voluntas quae supponitur libere operari?
pass_a_gloss: LXIII. Further, what the Doctors of the Reformed School confess, that the man who is converted through the grace of God freely elicits the first act of conversion itself, at first sight does not seem to agree well enough with what they commonly teach, and that with the Theologians of the Augsburg confession, namely, that man stands merely passively toward the work of his regeneration & conversion. For how can the human will freely elicit the act of conversion, & yet at the same time stand merely passively toward its own conversion? or does the will stand merely passively that is supposed to operate freely?
pass_b_english: Thesis LXIII. The Reformed teachers also admit that a person converted by God's grace freely performs the very first act of conversion. At first sight this does not seem to fit well with what they commonly teach, in agreement with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession: that in the work of his regeneration and conversion a person is merely passive.
How can the human will freely perform the act of conversion and yet be merely passive in its own conversion? Can a will that is assumed to act freely be merely passive?
